content: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a significant cause of lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) in infants. Maternal vaccination against RSV has emerged as a promising strategy to reduce the burden of RSV-related disease in infants. Recent advancements in the development of maternal RSV vaccines have accelerated clinical research in this area. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of maternal RSV vaccination in preventing RSV disease in infants. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases and trial registries was conducted, with the most recent update in July 2023. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing maternal RSV vaccination with placebo or no intervention in pregnant women were included. The primary outcomes assessed were infant hospitalizations due to laboratory-confirmed or clinically confirmed RSV disease. Secondary outcomes included adverse pregnancy outcomes (such as intrauterine growth restriction, stillbirth, and maternal death) and adverse infant outcomes (such as preterm birth, congenital abnormalities, and infant death). Six RCTs involving 17,991 pregnant women were included in the analysis. Four studies used an RSV pre-fusion (pre-F) protein vaccine, while two used an RSV F protein nanoparticle vaccine. All studies compared the vaccine to a placebo (saline, formulation buffer, or sterile water). Four studies were judged to have a low risk of bias, while two had a high risk of bias, primarily due to selection bias. All studies were funded by pharmaceutical companies. Maternal RSV vaccination was found to reduce the risk of infant hospitalization due to laboratory-confirmed RSV disease. The risk ratio (RR) was 0.50 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.31 to 0.82), based on high-certainty evidence from four RCTs involving 12,216 infants. This translates to 11 fewer hospitalizations per 1,000 infants born to vaccinated mothers, compared to those born to mothers who received a placebo. However, no studies reported on hospitalizations due to clinically confirmed RSV disease. The vaccine had little to no effect on the risk of congenital abnormalities, with a risk ratio of 0.96 (95% CI 0.88 to 1.04). This corresponds to five fewer congenital abnormalities per 1,000 infants (ranging from 17 fewer to six more), based on high-certainty evidence from four RCTs involving 12,304 infants. Maternal RSV vaccination likely had little to no effect on the risk of intrauterine growth restriction. The risk ratio was 1.32 (95% CI 0.75 to 2.33), based on moderate-certainty evidence from four RCTs involving 12,545 pregnant women. This corresponds to one additional case of intrauterine growth restriction per 1,000 pregnancies (ranging from one fewer to four more). The vaccine may have little to no effect on the risk of stillbirth, with a risk ratio of 0.81 (95% CI 0.38 to 1.72). This corresponds to no difference in stillbirth rates between vaccinated and placebo groups, based on data from five RCTs involving 12,652 pregnant women. There is a potential safety concern regarding preterm birth. Maternal RSV vaccination may increase the risk of preterm birth, although the evidence is very uncertain. The risk ratio was 1.16 (95% CI 0.99 to 1.36), based on very low-certainty evidence from six RCTs involving 17,560 infants. This corresponds to eight additional preterm births per 1,000 infants born to vaccinated mothers (ranging from one fewer to 18 more). This finding is primarily driven by data from a single trial that has not yet been fully published. There was one maternal death reported in the RSV vaccination group and none in the placebo group. The meta-analysis suggests that maternal RSV vaccination may have little to no effect on the risk of maternal death, with a risk ratio of 3.00 (95% CI 0.12 to 73.50), based on low-certainty evidence from three RCTs involving 7,977 pregnant women. The effect of maternal RSV vaccination on the risk of infant death is highly uncertain. The risk ratio was 0.81 (95% CI 0.36 to 1.81), based on very low-certainty evidence from six RCTs involving 17,589 infants. In conclusion, maternal RSV vaccination reduces the risk of infant hospitalizations due to laboratory-confirmed RSV disease. There are no significant safety concerns regarding intrauterine growth restriction or congenital abnormalities. However, the evidence for other safety outcomes, such as stillbirth, maternal death, and infant death, is of low or very low certainty. The potential association between maternal RSV vaccination and preterm birth warrants further investigation, particularly as this finding is based on limited and uncertain evidence. Future research should include larger RCTs and well-designed observational studies with long-term follow-up to better assess safety outcomes. Standardized outcome measures, data on concomitant vaccines, and stratification by timing of vaccination, gestational age at birth, race, and geographical setting are also needed to strengthen the evidence base.
